body:
The parent issue with description is #2690 

Proposed level changes for requirement in chapter "V10 Secure Coding Architecture and Implementation"

Full list of requirements for the chapter is listed here: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x18-V10-Coding.md

| # | Description | Level change |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **10.4.1** | [ADDED] Verify that the application explicitly ensures that variables are of the correct type and performs strict equality and comparator operations to avoid type juggling or type confusion vulnerabilities caused by the application code making an assumption about a variable type. | 1 > 2 |
| **10.4.2** | [ADDED] Verify that the application avoids DOM clobbering when using client-side JavaScript by employing explicit variable declarations, performing strict type checking, avoiding storing global variables on the document object, and implementing namespace isolation. | 2 > 3 |
| **10.4.4** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 5.1.2] Verify that the application has countermeasures to protect against mass assignment attacks by limiting allowed fields per controller and action, e.g., it is not possible to insert or update a field value when it was not intended to be part of that action. | 1 > 2 |
| **10.4.9** | [ADDED] Verify that, if the application (back-end or front-end) builds and sends requests, it uses validation, sanitization, or other mechanisms to avoid creating URIs (such as for API calls) or HTTP request header fields (such as Authorization or Cookie), which are too long to be accepted by the receiving component. This could cause a denial of service, such as when sending an overly long request (e.g. a long cookie header field) results in the server always responding with an error status. | 2 > 3 |
| **10.6.2** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 10.3.2] Verify that third-party components and all of their transitive dependencies are included from the expected repository, whether internally owned or an external source, and that there is no risk of a dependency confusion attack. | 1 > 3 |
| **10.7.3** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 11.1.6] Verify that all access to shared resources is consistently checked and accessed in a single atomic operation to prevent Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race conditions, ensuring resource state consistency between check and use. | 2 > 3 |

comments.body:
10.4.1 can be a really big problem in financial services. I suggest keeping it as level 1.

| # | Description | Level change |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **10.4.1** | [ADDED] Verify that the application explicitly ensures that variables are of the correct type and performs strict equality and comparator operations to avoid type juggling or type confusion vulnerabilities caused by the application code making an assumption about a variable type. | 1 > 2 |

10.4.4 is easy for developers to get right and if they do not it's a very high impact event. I suggest leaving it at level 1. And admittedly, this does not apply to most languages. It's mostly a rails issue.

| # | Description | Level change |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **10.4.4** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 5.1.2] Verify that the application has countermeasures to protect against mass assignment attacks by limiting allowed fields per controller and action, e.g., it is not possible to insert or update a field value when it was not intended to be part of that action. | 1 > 2 |

For 10.6.2 supply chain attacks are on the rise. I'd suggest at least keeping it as level 2.

| # | Description | Level change |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **10.6.2** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 10.3.2] Verify that third-party components and all of their transitive dependencies are included from the expected repository, whether internally owned or an external source, and that there is no risk of a dependency confusion attack. | 1 > 3 |

10.4.1 is quite hard to justify to "with having only this problem, your application is vulnerable", taking into account there is also input validation in place.

10.4.4 high impact comes when there is a problem with field level authorization controls. mass-assignment is just a control to be sure that the application does not accept input via controls that are not expecting those fields. We have field level authorization as level 2 (your own proposal, if I remember correctly), it would not be aligned with that as well.

10.6.2 is it a basic level security **every** application must satisfy or is it a step further?

> 10.4.1 is quite hard to justify to "with having only this problem, your application is vulnerable", taking into account there is also input validation in place.

I agree, I think that's totally fair.

> 10.4.4 high impact comes when there is a problem with field level authorization controls. mass-assignment is just a control to be sure that the application does not accept input via controls that are not expecting those fields. We have field level authorization as level 2 (your own proposal, if I remember correctly), it would not be aligned with that as well.

The only reason I question this is because it's a niche problem in Rails and not common to all apps.

> 10.6.2 is it a basic level security **every** application must satisfy or is it a step further?

I think that's a fair argument.

The only one I am still concerned about is 10.4.4 because it's so niche and not a problem in most frameworks and languages.

Jim, I think you over-estimate the importance of 10.4.4 as a separate requirement.

> V10.4.4 Verify that the application has countermeasures to protect against mass assignment attacks by limiting allowed fields per controller and action, e.g., **it is not possible to insert or update a field value when it was not intended to be part of that action**.

The key point here is that it only addresses "you should not be able to insert or update a field value from certain action," even if you have permission to update the same field via some other form. In case you don't have permission, you need to have a  missing field level authorization check as a precondition, and I think this is your actual focus here:
> V4.1.7 Verify that the application ensures that field-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific fields to mitigate broken object property level authorization (BOPLA).

So if you have only problem with V10.4.4 in your application (without authorization problems from 4.1.*), you are quite ok actually.

I read up on mass assignment for 10.4.4 more and as you are suggesting this affects any ORB type framework. I'm convinced you are right.

When 10.6.2 happens it's globally bad. I'd at least suggest it's L2. This seems important for every app.

I'll hold off, I support you making the final call on these.

> Jim, I think you over-estimate the importance of 10.4.4 as a separate requirement.

I’m a little confused. Just to make sure I’m clear, I don’t think this is super important for all apps. I wanted to demote it. Mostly. 

Did you mean over-estimate or under-estimate?

And I’m flexible on this, I just don’t see it often. Maybe you see something different and that’s cool with me.

> Did you mean over-estimate or under-estimate?

From your initial statement
> 10.4.4 is easy for developers to get right and if they do not it's a very high impact event. **I suggest leaving it at level 1**. And admittedly, this does not apply to most languages. It's mostly a rails issue.

If you suggest to keep it at L1 one can conclude you find it quite important and my opinion for this is, that you maybe over-estimate the importance for it.

For me, 10.4.4 is a clear L2 and therefore I move forward with PR.

If there is a need to discuss or explain the reasoning further, we can reopen a separate issue for that.
10.4.1 and 10.4.4 seem borderline between L1 and L2 but I think they are slightly more unusual than some other L1 examples and we have a limit on what we can include...
I am ok to let this go and remain a closed issue. Moving on. All good.
